title: Streetwear Layering: How to Dress Warm Without Looking Bulky
description: Layering isn't stacking five hoodies. Here's how to build a winter fit that handles -5°C outside and doesn't cook you the second you get on the train.
excerpt: Three layers, three different lengths, one colour line. Done right, a winter fit beats a summer one — and you don't have to freeze for it.
content:
Winter fits fail in one specific way: you pile on pieces that don't know about each other. The result is a loaf. Layering actually runs on a simple rule — every layer gets a different length, a different weight and a different job.

## Three layers, three lengths

The base is thin: a long-sleeve tee or a light crewneck. The middle does the warming — a hoodie or a fleece. The outer layer is a wind shield: a jacket, a parka, a puffer.

Length is the whole trick. If the tee runs a couple of inches past the hoodie and the jacket sits noticeably higher or lower, you get layering that reads as intentional. If all three hems land at the same spot, you just look like someone who's cold.

## Materials that get along

Cotton on skin, fleece or a hoodie in the middle, nylon or wool on top. What doesn't work: two heavy cotton hoodies stacked. They soak up sweat, stop insulating, and add bulk exactly where you don't want it — around the arms.

Keep it to three tones max. A neutral base (black, grey, sand) plus one accent — a red beanie, an orange lining, a loud shoe.

## The zip is your thermostat

The most practical winter trick: make at least one layer a full zip. Open it on the train, close it on the street. A mid-weight zip jacket beats the warmest pullover that has no way to vent.

Pieces that stack like this — from base hoodies to outerwear — are what [DOPESTORE](https://dopestore.cz) is built around. Start with one neutral jacket that goes over everything; the rest of the fit assembles itself.
